title: Assessing leadership of change and stakeholder engagement
blurb: Judge how well a project leads people from the current to the target state: hidden stakeholders, key influencers, resistance, culture and co-creation.
question: A respected senior nurse who took part in a failed earlier attempt is openly sceptical of a new triage hub. The project manager leaves him out of the design group so he will not unsettle others. Is this appropriate, and why?

teach.body: In PRINCE2 7, change management is how an organization moves from its current state to a target state, often through interim states. The project delivers products; people have to change how they work for the benefits to appear. Leading that change means finding everyone affected or influential, understanding resistance rather than overriding it, keeping ways of working aligned with the culture, and co-creating with the people who will live with the result.

teach.h: Current to target state at Wenmoor (S3)

steps.label: Current state
steps.sub: 14 referral routes, 9 days to first contact

teach.caption: The change management approach describes each state and the enabling activities before, during and after the transition.

teach.body: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect, is affected by, or PERCEIVES itself to be affected by the project. Identify stakeholders and key influencers, including key people who are impacted or critical to success but hold no formal role. Relationships change over time. Build relationships across interfaces through regular meetings and working groups that create a shared understanding of perspectives, data and agreed knowledge, and set ways of working that keep impacted areas involved.

cells.label: Affected groups, those who feel affected

teach.caption: The top-right box is the one weak stakeholder analyses miss: informal leaders and outside opinion-formers with no project role.

teach.body: Pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused: find out WHY someone resists, as they may have a valid point, instead of sidelining them. Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices. Gather feedback and act on it so the agreed ways of working stay aligned with how people actually work. Persistent non-compliance with project processes is a leading indicator that the ways of working no longer fit the emerging culture.

root.label: People resist or keep not complying

children.label: Weak
children.sub: The reason stays hidden and resistance grows

children.label: Adjust with them
children.sub: Co-create the product or way of working

children.label: Focus communication
children.sub: Target the message where resistance sits

teach.body: Co-creation is a form of collaboration that involves users and key influencers in designing products and agreed ways of working, so that they are adopted. Co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities unites their perspectives, improves development and adoption, reduces handover risk and makes sure operating needs are considered. People are also more willing to work in ways they helped to shape.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Wenmoor Single Point of Access (S3)
items: Many district nurses fear a triage hub will take away their professional judgement, and a 2021 attempt in Moorside was abandoned without anyone recording why.
Ellie Chandran (PM) names Gareth Pugh, a senior nurse with no project role whom many follow, and the Moorside GP federation chair as key influencers, and meets both to understand their concerns.
She invites nurses from each locality and the patients' forum to co-design draft triage criteria, which then go to the clinical safety officer and medical director for sign-off.
When pilot staff keep skipping a referral log, she asks why, simplifies it with them and records the change: acting on feedback so ways of working fit the culture.

teach.text: Change MANAGEMENT (people moving from current to target state, people element) is not change CONTROL (decisions on changes to baselines, issues practice). An option that sends a people problem off to a request for change or the issue register is usually a distractor.

items: Change management moves the organization from current to target state, through any interim states.
Identify stakeholders and key influencers, including people with no formal role and those who only perceive an effect.
Investigate resistance; it shows where to focus communication.
Act on feedback: persistent non-compliance signals that ways of working no longer fit the culture.
Co-create products and ways of working with users and key influencers to improve adoption.

summary: You can now judge whether a project leads change well: finding hidden stakeholders and key influencers, investigating resistance, acting on feedback about ways of working, building shared understanding across interfaces and co-creating with the people affected. You can also keep change management apart from change control.

A.q: On Calderbrook's permit project, the stakeholder analysis lists the board, the supplier, the head of parking services and the contact centre manager. It does not mention a permit officer with 20 years' service who designed many of the team's workarounds and whom colleagues ask for advice. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask the head of parking services to brief him when the design is final
Record him in the risk register as a possible source of resistance
Name him as a key influencer and involve him in designing the new process
Leave him off the analysis, since he holds no formal role in the project
A.why: Stakeholder engagement identifies key influencers, including key people who are critical to success but hold no formal role (3.2.2), and co-creation involves them in designing products and ways of working (3.3).

whyNot.0: Briefing him after the design is final misses the chance to use his knowledge and gain his support.
whyNot.1: A risk entry may be sensible, but it does not engage him; the people element calls for involvement.
whyNot.3: Key influencers often hold no formal role; that is exactly why they must be identified.

A.q: On Carrowford's half marathon, the vicar of a church on the route has organized a joint letter from local churches objecting to the road closures. The cabinet member suggests not replying because the route is fixed. The project manager instead meets the clergy to understand their concerns, such as service times and access for older worshippers. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because resistance shows where to focus, and its reasons should be understood
Yes, because a meeting will let her persuade the churches the route cannot change
No, because the route is fixed, so the churches' views cannot alter the project
No, because the objection should first be logged and assessed as an issue
A.why: Pockets of resistance are a useful indicator of where communication should be focused; the reasons should be investigated, as they may be valid (3.4, 3.2.2).

whyNot.1: The aim is to understand the concerns, which may lead to adjustments such as timing at those points, not simply to persuade.
whyNot.2: A fixed route still leaves room to address concerns, and ignoring a key stakeholder group risks the event's reputation.
whyNot.3: Recording it may also happen, but logging an issue does not engage the churches or uncover their reasons.

A.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the member services teams, the IT operations staff and the cloud partner each have a different view of when application switch-overs can safely happen. The project manager sets up a fortnightly working group with people from all three to agree a shared view of the application data and the switch-over windows. Which statement explains why this is appropriate?
options: Change authority should be delegated to a group that can approve changes
Working groups across interfaces build a shared understanding of the data
The project board should include member services, IT and the supplier
Project assurance should check the switch-over windows independently
A.why: Relationship building across interfaces can be done through regular meetings and working groups that build a shared understanding of different perspectives, the project data and agreed knowledge (3.2.2).

whyNot.0: A change authority approves requests for change within limits; this group exists to build shared understanding.
whyNot.2: Board composition is an organizing decision; the working group is not a board.
whyNot.3: Assurance may review the plan, but it does not explain why the three groups need to work together.

B.q: At Wenmoor Community Health, pilot team members keep failing to complete a new referral-tracking spreadsheet, saying it takes too long between home visits. The project manager meets them, simplifies the spreadsheet with them and records the revised way of working. How well does this apply the guidance on leading successful change, and why?
options: It applies it well, because project support should complete the spreadsheet for them
It applies it poorly, because a change to a procedure needs an approved request for change
It applies it poorly, because staff should be reminded to follow the agreed procedure
It applies it well, because persistent non-compliance shows the way of working no longer fits
B.why: Feedback should be acted on so that defined ways of working stay aligned with how people actually work; persistent non-compliance is a leading indicator that they no longer fit the emerging culture (3.2.3).

whyNot.0: Project support provides admin services, but handing the task over does not explain why acting on the feedback is right.
whyNot.1: A tracking spreadsheet is not a baselined product needing change control; the people element calls for acting on the feedback.
whyNot.2: Reminders treat the symptom; the repeated non-compliance is telling the PM the process does not fit.

B.q: On Carrowford's half marathon, residents on the route are complaining on social media that they cannot drive out of their streets for five hours. The project manager's stakeholder analysis left them out because they 'are not formally part of the event'. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because residents hold no formal role in planning or running the event
Yes, because complaints on social media are for the council's press office
No, because stakeholders include people who are, or feel, affected by the project
No, because residents on the route should be given a place on the project board
B.why: A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the project (3.2.2). The residents clearly qualify.

whyNot.0: A formal role is not the test; affected people without a role are stakeholders.
whyNot.1: The press office may help with messages, but the project still needs to identify and engage these stakeholders.
whyNot.3: Engaging stakeholders does not mean putting them on the board; the board holds business, user and supplier roles.

B.q: At Fernhollow Foods the new tray-sealing line will change the night shift's routines, with new allergen controls and new shift patterns. The project manager sets out training before the line goes live, extra supervisors during the first weeks and a help line for operators afterwards. Where should this be recorded?
options: In the issue management approach, because it controls changes to baselines
In the change management approach, as activities to enable the transition
In the quality management approach, because allergen controls are standards
In the communication management approach, so operators are told of changes
B.why: The change management approach describes how the business moves from current to target state, including enabling activities before, during and after transition, such as training, trials and a help line (3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The issue management approach covers change control of baselines, not helping people adopt new ways of working.
whyNot.2: Allergen standards belong in quality planning, but training, supervision and a help line are transition activities.
whyNot.3: Operators will need to be told, but the activities described are enabling the transition, not a communication schedule.

C.q: At Wenmoor Community Health many district nurses fear that central triage will take away their professional judgement. The project manager invites nurses from each locality, including an influential sceptic, and patients' forum members to co-design draft triage criteria, which will then go to the clinical safety officer and medical director for sign-off. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the nurses can then approve the triage criteria among themselves
Yes, because co-creating with users and key influencers improves adoption
No, because the medical director is the person who must approve the criteria
No, because involving sceptical nurses will slow down the design of the criteria
C.why: Co-creation involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working so they are adopted (3.3), and co-creating products improves adoption and reduces handover risk (3.5.1). Sign-off still follows the trust's rules.

whyNot.0: The nurses design a draft; the clinical safety officer and medical director still sign it off.
whyNot.2: The medical director does approve the criteria, and the plan respects that; it is not a reason to avoid co-design.
whyNot.3: Involving sceptics may take longer, but it addresses the fear that threatens adoption.

C.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, a senior systems engineer with 18 years in the data centres is an informal leader of the operations staff and openly sceptical of the move. The project manager leaves him out of the operations working group because she thinks he will unsettle others. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the working group should stay positive to build social cohesion
Yes, because his line manager can pass the group's decisions on to him
No, because he should be made senior user to represent the operations staff
No, because key influencers should be engaged and their resistance explored
C.why: Key influencers must be identified and engaged (3.2.2), and resistance shows where communication should focus so its reasons can be understood (3.4). Excluding him leaves the resistance untouched.

whyNot.0: Cohesion built by excluding an influential sceptic will not survive contact with the staff who follow him.
whyNot.1: Passing decisions on second-hand does not engage him or uncover his reasons.
whyNot.2: The senior user represents those who will use the outputs and is a board role; engagement does not require a board seat.

C.q: On Calderbrook's permit project, the change management approach describes the current paper process and the target online service, but plans no interim state: the paper route would close on the day the private beta starts in one ward, with no parallel running. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because one switch-over avoids the cost of running two processes
Yes, because the benefits in the business case depend on the target state
No, because closing the paper process needs an approved request for change
No, because the approach should show the move through any interim states
C.why: The change management approach sets out the target state and how the business will move from the current state through any interim states (3.2.1). A private beta in one ward is an interim state that needs planning.

whyNot.0: Cost matters, but a one-day switch with no interim state ignores how people will actually make the transition.
whyNot.1: The benefits do depend on the target state, which is why the route there must be planned with care.
whyNot.2: This is a people transition question for the change management approach, not change control.

reteach.title: Find them, hear them, involve them
reteach.question: Think of the people who could quietly sink this change. Have you found them, listened to them and given them a hand in shaping it?

blocks.body: FIND: list everyone who is, or feels, affected, plus the influencers with no project role. HEAR: when people resist or ignore a process, ask why; their reasons tell you where to focus and what to fix. INVOLVE: co-create products and ways of working with the people who will use them, so they adopt the result. Then plan the journey from current to target state, including any interim states.

steps.label: Involve
steps.sub: Co-create products and ways of working

blocks.text: Sidelining a sceptic, waiting to brief people until the design is final, or answering non-compliance with reminders all look tidy and are all weak answers.

explain.body: Change management moves people and the organization to a target state. Change control decides on changes to baselined products and sits in the issues practice. Same word, different jobs.

test.q: At Tarnside College two matters come up in stage 2. The vice principal asks for 30 welding bays instead of the 24 in the approved design. Separately, instructors who have taught in classrooms will need to move to workshop-based teaching with new routines and responsibilities. Which matter should the change management approach address, and why?
options: The request for more bays, because it changes the approved design baseline
Both matters, because each one is a change to what the project will deliver
Neither matter, because both should be raised and decided through the issue register
The instructors' move, because it is a shift in routines towards the target state
test.why: Change management is about the organization moving from current to target state, including changes to routines, practices and responsibilities (3.2.1). The extra bays are a request for change under the issues practice.

whyNot.0: A change to the approved design is change control in the issues practice, not change management.
whyNot.1: The instructors' move is a people transition; the bay request is a baseline change. They belong to different approaches.
whyNot.2: The bay request does go through issue handling, but the instructors' transition is a people matter for change management.

explain.body: Some of the most important people hold no formal role: informal leaders, professional bodies, community figures. Identify them early and engage them, because relationships and opinions shape whether the change lands.

test.q: At Wenmoor Community Health, the chair of the rural GP federation, who is influential with practices in that locality, has publicly questioned whether the single point of access is needed there. Several practices say they will keep faxing referrals to nurses they know. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Meet the chair as a key influencer to understand the federation's concerns
Ask the commissioner to require the practices to use the new referral route
Record the fax referrals as a problem in the issue register and wait
Plan the rural roll-out without the GPs, as they are outside the trust
test.why: Stakeholder engagement identifies key influencers and builds relationships with them (3.2.2); her public resistance shows where communication should be focused (3.4).

whyNot.1: A requirement from above does not build understanding and may harden resistance in a locality that already doubts the change.
whyNot.2: It may be logged, but waiting does nothing to engage the person whose view the practices follow.
whyNot.3: GPs are stakeholders who affect the project's success; being outside the trust does not remove them.

explain.body: Pockets of resistance tell you where to focus communication. Find out why: the person may have a valid point that improves the product.

test.q: On Calderbrook's permit project, the head of parking services, who will run the new service, says she doubts an online-only service will work for her customers. The project manager meets her to find out why and learns that many older residents phone in. The design then keeps a telephone assisted route. Which statement explains why the project manager's action is appropriate?
options: Senior users should be appointed from the people who will run the service
Pockets of resistance show where to focus, and the reasons may be valid
Requests for change should be weighed against their cost and their risk
Lessons from the council's earlier app should be built into this design
test.why: Pockets of resistance indicate where communication should be focused, and investigating the reasons can reveal valid concerns (3.4). Here it led to a better design.

whyNot.0: She may well be a good senior user, but the action described is investigating her resistance.
whyNot.2: Weighing changes is part of justification; the stem is about understanding a stakeholder's objection.
whyNot.3: Using earlier lessons is learn from experience; nothing in the stem draws on the earlier app.

explain.body: Where groups meet, misunderstandings grow. Regular meetings and working groups build a shared view of perspectives, data and agreed knowledge, and ways of working that keep every impacted area involved.

test.q: At Fernhollow Foods, the technical team and the co-manufacturer keep disagreeing about how allergen test results should be recorded and shared. The project manager sets up a joint working group that meets every fortnight to agree one data format and how the two sites will work together. Which statement explains why this is appropriate?
options: Regular working groups across interfaces build shared understanding and ways of working
Structured team-building exercises can speed up the forming of a new project team
Quality control checks that products meet their quality specifications
The commercial management approach sets out how suppliers will be managed
test.why: Relationship building across interfaces, through regular meetings and working groups, builds a shared understanding of perspectives, data and agreed knowledge, and supports agreed ways of working (3.2.2).

whyNot.1: This is an ongoing working group at an interface, not a one-off team-building exercise.
whyNot.2: Allergen testing is quality control, but the action is about agreeing how two organizations share data.
whyNot.3: The commercial approach covers supplier management, but it does not explain why a joint working group is appropriate here.
